options.action: Do not initiate or progress structured exercise or intradialytic exercise at this time; manage unstable condition first and follow standard haemodialysis care without added exercise.

options.action: Delay starting intradialytic cycling until after the first 30 minutes of haemodialysis, then perform supervised intradialytic cycling for at least 30 minutes at a moderate intensity (Borg RPE 12–14) on each haemodialysis treatment (3 times/week), and encourage additional physical activity on non-dialysis days aiming toward a total of 150 minutes/week of moderate activity (or 75 minutes vigorous).

options.label: C
options.action: Provide supervised intradialytic cycling during this haemodialysis session for at least 30 minutes at a moderate intensity (Borg RPE 12–14) on each treatment (3 times/week) to improve cardiovascular health, physical function, muscular strength, blood pressure control, lipid profile and dialysis efficiency, and encourage additional interdialytic physical activity toward 150 minutes/week of moderate activity (or 75 minutes vigorous).

options.label: D
options.action: Encourage haemodialysis patient to perform regular physical activity outside dialysis (e.g. home-based walking or other moderate-intensity activity) aiming for 150 minutes/week of moderate intensity (or 75 minutes vigorous, or a mixture), with programmes ideally supervised by appropriately qualified staff when available, while addressing individual patient and staff barriers to optimise participation and adherence.

options.label: E
options.action: Avoid contact sports and activities with high risk of traumatic graft damage, avoid prolonged extreme endurance events unless carefully considered with a transplant and sports medicine team, and avoid sport‑enhancing dietary supplements; otherwise encourage only moderate, non-contact physical activity within standard guidelines.

options.label: F
options.action: Do not implement additional intensive physiotherapy or structured exercise beyond standard early mobility encouragement; continue standard care mobilization without extra intensive exercise, as early intensive physiotherapy has not shown added benefit.

options.label: G
options.action: Offer prehabilitation: encourage and, if possible, supervise structured cardiovascular and strength exercise (at least 3 times per week) to increase pre-transplant physical activity levels and potentially aid recovery post-transplant, aiming for at least 150 minutes/week of moderate‑to‑vigorous physical activity (or 75 minutes vigorous).

options.label: H
options.action: Implement a supervised, individualised structured exercise programme performed at least 3 times/week, including aerobic exercise at >60% of maximum (heart rate or VO2peak) and resistance training of upper and lower body at >60% 1-RM at least 2 times/week, progressing volume gradually, to enhance cardiorespiratory fitness, muscular strength, physical function, HDL levels and health-related quality of life while aiming for ≥150 minutes/week of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity.

options.label: I
options.action: Encourage general physical activity toward 150 minutes/week of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (or 75 minutes vigorous), aiming to reduce all‑cause and cardiovascular mortality and improve functional outcomes, and address individual barriers and activators to increase uptake; structured exercise can be advised but may be unsupervised or adapted to the patient’s circumstances.

options.label: J
options.action: Do not prescribe progressive exercise beyond gentle activity; manage contraindications and stabilise comorbidities first, while offering only cautious basic physical activity as tolerated.

options.label: K
options.action: Advise the patient to maintain current aerobic activity levels (≥150 minutes/week moderate or 75 minutes vigorous), ensure participation in muscle strength, balance and flexibility activities on at least 2 days per week, and minimise sedentary time by breaking up prolonged sitting; a prescribed combination of aerobic and muscle strengthening should be used to improve or maintain muscle function, blood pressure, physical function, and quality of life.

options.label: L
options.action: Encourage the patient to gradually increase physical activity from current levels toward 150 minutes/week of moderate intensity aerobic activity (or 75 minutes vigorous, or combination), participate in daily physical activity, undertake strength, balance and flexibility activities at least 2 days per week, and break up prolonged sedentary periods with light activity or standing; use a prescribed combination of aerobic and muscle strengthening to improve muscle function, blood pressure, physical function, and health-related quality of life.

options.label: M
options.action: The patient does not fall into the specified CKD non-dialysis, haemodialysis, or transplant groups covered by this guideline; apply other appropriate clinical guidelines.

options.label: N
options.action: This guideline does not apply because the patient does not have chronic kidney disease or kidney replacement therapy.

options.label: O
options.action: Insufficient explicit patient evidence to select a guideline recommendation.

options.action: Do not initiate or progress structured exercise or intradialytic exercise at this time; manage unstable condition first and follow standard haemodialysis care without added exercise.

options.label: B
options.action: Delay starting intradialytic cycling until after the first 30 minutes of haemodialysis, then perform supervised intradialytic cycling for at least 30 minutes at a moderate intensity (Borg RPE 12–14) on each haemodialysis treatment (3 times/week), and encourage additional physical activity on non-dialysis days aiming toward a total of 150 minutes/week of moderate activity (or 75 minutes vigorous).

options.label: C
options.action: Provide supervised intradialytic cycling during this haemodialysis session for at least 30 minutes at a moderate intensity (Borg RPE 12–14) on each treatment (3 times/week) to improve cardiovascular health, physical function, muscular strength, blood pressure control, lipid profile and dialysis efficiency, and encourage additional interdialytic physical activity toward 150 minutes/week of moderate activity (or 75 minutes vigorous).

options.label: D
options.action: Encourage haemodialysis patient to perform regular physical activity outside dialysis (e.g. home-based walking or other moderate-intensity activity) aiming for 150 minutes/week of moderate intensity (or 75 minutes vigorous, or a mixture), with programmes ideally supervised by appropriately qualified staff when available, while addressing individual patient and staff barriers to optimise participation and adherence.

options.label: E
options.action: Avoid contact sports and activities with high risk of traumatic graft damage, avoid prolonged extreme endurance events unless carefully considered with a transplant and sports medicine team, and avoid sport‑enhancing dietary supplements; otherwise encourage only moderate, non-contact physical activity within standard guidelines.

options.label: F
options.action: Do not implement additional intensive physiotherapy or structured exercise beyond standard early mobility encouragement; continue standard care mobilization without extra intensive exercise, as early intensive physiotherapy has not shown added benefit.

options.label: G
options.action: Offer prehabilitation: encourage and, if possible, supervise structured cardiovascular and strength exercise (at least 3 times per week) to increase pre-transplant physical activity levels and potentially aid recovery post-transplant, aiming for at least 150 minutes/week of moderate‑to‑vigorous physical activity (or 75 minutes vigorous).

options.label: H
options.action: Implement a supervised, individualised structured exercise programme performed at least 3 times/week, including aerobic exercise at >60% of maximum (heart rate or VO2peak) and resistance training of upper and lower body at >60% 1-RM at least 2 times/week, progressing volume gradually, to enhance cardiorespiratory fitness, muscular strength, physical function, HDL levels and health-related quality of life while aiming for ≥150 minutes/week of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity.

options.label: I
options.action: Encourage general physical activity toward 150 minutes/week of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (or 75 minutes vigorous), aiming to reduce all‑cause and cardiovascular mortality and improve functional outcomes, and address individual barriers and activators to increase uptake; structured exercise can be advised but may be unsupervised or adapted to the patient’s circumstances.

options.label: J
options.action: Do not prescribe progressive exercise beyond gentle activity; manage contraindications and stabilise comorbidities first, while offering only cautious basic physical activity as tolerated.

options.label: K
options.action: Advise the patient to maintain current aerobic activity levels (≥150 minutes/week moderate or 75 minutes vigorous), ensure participation in muscle strength, balance and flexibility activities on at least 2 days per week, and minimise sedentary time by breaking up prolonged sitting; a prescribed combination of aerobic and muscle strengthening should be used to improve or maintain muscle function, blood pressure, physical function, and quality of life.

options.label: L
options.action: Encourage the patient to gradually increase physical activity from current levels toward 150 minutes/week of moderate intensity aerobic activity (or 75 minutes vigorous, or combination), participate in daily physical activity, undertake strength, balance and flexibility activities at least 2 days per week, and break up prolonged sedentary periods with light activity or standing; use a prescribed combination of aerobic and muscle strengthening to improve muscle function, blood pressure, physical function, and health-related quality of life.

options.label: M
options.action: The patient does not fall into the specified CKD non-dialysis, haemodialysis, or transplant groups covered by this guideline; apply other appropriate clinical guidelines.

options.label: N
options.action: This guideline does not apply because the patient does not have chronic kidney disease or kidney replacement therapy.

options.label: O
options.action: Insufficient explicit patient evidence to select a guideline recommendation.

options.label: A
options.action: Provide oral nutritional supplementation (including between-meal snacks where appropriate) over a short term (about 3–12 weeks) to increase energy intake and modestly improve body weight, BMI and malnutrition status in the person with dementia.

options.label: B
options.action: Provide rich finger foods as a pragmatic approach to enhance consumption and total food intake for the person with dementia in the institutional setting.

options.label: C
options.action: Consider other non-pharmacological approaches (such as assistance with eating and drinking, person-centered mealtime care, environmental modification, and education or training) to address feeding and eating disorders and related nutritional problems in this person with dementia.

options.label: D
options.action: Provide assistance with eating and drinking using under hand and/or direct hand feeding techniques, allowing sufficient time to finish meals, to increase meal intake and reduce feeding problem behaviors.

options.label: E
options.action: Provide assistance with eating and drinking using available handfeeding techniques, allowing sufficient time to finish meals, recognizing that over hand feeding may be associated with more frequent feeding problem behaviors.

options.label: F
options.action: Implement a high-quality improvement system to organize and manage mealtime feeding assistance so that staff provide more consistent assistance, helping to improve meal intake and reduce unintentional weight loss among persons with dementia.

options.label: G
options.action: Use assistive devices or technologies that support meal preparation (e.g., technologies enabling beginning or carrying on cooking) to help the person with dementia initiate and maintain cooking and food preparation.

options.label: H
options.action: Emphasize person-centered mealtime care, environmental modification, and caregiver education or training to address behavioral and engagement-related feeding and eating problems in the person with dementia.

options.label: I
options.action: Implement spaced retrieval training and/or Montessori-based activities to improve hyperphagic, rapid eating, pica and other eating-related behaviors, enhance self-eating ability, and increase meal intake, with possible long-term benefits.

options.label: J
options.action: Provide non-pharmacological individual therapeutic-cognitive intervention (cognitive-behavioral education) directed to family caregivers to improve control and reduction of eating disorders in the person with dementia.

options.label: K
options.action: Provide intensive and longer-term education, counselling, or training on nutrition, feeding skills, and prevention of weight loss for caregivers and/or the person with dementia, using available formats (e.g., face-to-face or web-based) to slightly improve food intake and body weight.

options.label: L
options.action: Use spaced retrieval training with a visual aid to improve 2–3 compensatory swallowing behaviors in the person with dementia during eating and drinking.

options.label: M
options.action: Focus on environmental modification and person-centered mealtime care (e.g., pleasant and home-like environments, tailored care and choices) to improve engagement with eating and mealtime experience in this mildly affected person with dementia.

options.label: N
options.action: Use a multi-component, individualized management approach combining interventions such as oral nutritional supplementation, food or drink modification and assistance, environmental modification, psychomotor or behavioral programs, and caregiver training, based on a geriatric assessment and, where available, recommendations from a multidisciplinary mobile dementia team.

options.label: O
options.action: No specific non-pharmacological feeding and eating disorder intervention from this guideline is required at this time; continue general dementia care, monitor for emergence of feeding and eating disorders, and reassess if such problems develop.

options.label: P
options.action: Insufficient explicit patient evidence to select a guideline recommendation.

options.label: A
options.action: Provide oral nutritional supplementation (including between-meal snacks where appropriate) over a short term (about 3–12 weeks) to increase energy intake and modestly improve body weight, BMI and malnutrition status in the person with dementia.

options.label: B
options.action: Provide rich finger foods as a pragmatic approach to enhance consumption and total food intake for the person with dementia in the institutional setting.

options.label: C
options.action: Consider other non-pharmacological approaches (such as assistance with eating and drinking, person-centered mealtime care, environmental modification, and education or training) to address feeding and eating disorders and related nutritional problems in this person with dementia.

options.label: D
options.action: Provide assistance with eating and drinking using under hand and/or direct hand feeding techniques, allowing sufficient time to finish meals, to increase meal intake and reduce feeding problem behaviors.

options.label: E
options.action: Provide assistance with eating and drinking using available handfeeding techniques, allowing sufficient time to finish meals, recognizing that over hand feeding may be associated with more frequent feeding problem behaviors.

options.label: F
options.action: Implement a high-quality improvement system to organize and manage mealtime feeding assistance so that staff provide more consistent assistance, helping to improve meal intake and reduce unintentional weight loss among persons with dementia.

options.label: G
options.action: Use assistive devices or technologies that support meal preparation (e.g., technologies enabling beginning or carrying on cooking) to help the person with dementia initiate and maintain cooking and food preparation.

options.label: H
options.action: Emphasize person-centered mealtime care, environmental modification, and caregiver education or training to address behavioral and engagement-related feeding and eating problems in the person with dementia.

options.label: I
options.action: Implement spaced retrieval training and/or Montessori-based activities to improve hyperphagic, rapid eating, pica and other eating-related behaviors, enhance self-eating ability, and increase meal intake, with possible long-term benefits.

options.label: J
options.action: Provide non-pharmacological individual therapeutic-cognitive intervention (cognitive-behavioral education) directed to family caregivers to improve control and reduction of eating disorders in the person with dementia.

options.label: K
options.action: Provide intensive and longer-term education, counselling, or training on nutrition, feeding skills, and prevention of weight loss for caregivers and/or the person with dementia, using available formats (e.g., face-to-face or web-based) to slightly improve food intake and body weight.

options.label: L
options.action: Use spaced retrieval training with a visual aid to improve 2–3 compensatory swallowing behaviors in the person with dementia during eating and drinking.

options.label: M
options.action: Focus on environmental modification and person-centered mealtime care (e.g., pleasant and home-like environments, tailored care and choices) to improve engagement with eating and mealtime experience in this mildly affected person with dementia.

options.label: N
options.action: Use a multi-component, individualized management approach combining interventions such as oral nutritional supplementation, food or drink modification and assistance, environmental modification, psychomotor or behavioral programs, and caregiver training, based on a geriatric assessment and, where available, recommendations from a multidisciplinary mobile dementia team.

options.label: O
options.action: No specific non-pharmacological feeding and eating disorder intervention from this guideline is required at this time; continue general dementia care, monitor for emergence of feeding and eating disorders, and reassess if such problems develop.

options.label: P
options.action: Insufficient explicit patient evidence to select a guideline recommendation.

options.label: I

options.label: J

options.label: K

options.label: L

options.label: M
options.action: Resect recurrent tumor whenever possible, using techniques emphasizing complete margin assessment; consider adjuvant radiation therapy if margins are positive/indeterminate and further resection is not feasible.

options.label: N

options.label: O
options.action: Recurrent, unresectable tumor without prior RT: use definitive radiation therapy (50–60 Gy for indeterminate/positive margins, up to 66 Gy for gross tumor) as primary local treatment.

options.label: P
